title: A legendary nebula
caption: The Crab Nebula (Messier 1), imaged by the Mayall 4-meter Telescope
celestial: M1, NGC 1952 · constellation Taurus · about 6500 light-years away (source figure)
credit: KPNO/NOIRLab/NSF/AURA · Image Processing: T.A. Rector (University of Alaska Anchorage/NSF NOIRLab)

recognition.text: NOIRLab Image of the Week (an editorial selection, not an audience score).

story: This portrait of Messier 1, the Crab Nebula, comes from the Nicholas U. Mayall 4-meter Telescope at NSF NOIRLab's Kitt Peak National Observatory (KPNO). The Crab is a supernova remnant, the spreading debris of a star that exploded.

Its history runs through modern astronomy. British astronomer John Bevis recorded it in 1731 and took it for a cloudy blob. More than three decades later the French comet hunter Charles Messier showed it was a real object, and it became the first entry in his catalogue of nebulae and star clusters. In the early 20th century, astronomers tied it to a supernova that Chinese astronomers had seen in 1054, making it the first object linked to a previously recorded supernova.

In 1968 astronomers found a pulsar inside the nebula at radio wavelengths. A pulsar is the ultra-dense, fast-spinning core left behind by the star. A year later John Cocke, Donald Taylor and Michael Disney confirmed it in visible light using KPNO's UArizona 0.9-meter Spacewatch Telescope.
scale: Using the source's listed field of view (16.74 x 11.77 arcminutes) and distance (6500 light years), the frame spans roughly 32 × 22 light-years. Its light set out about 6,500 years before reaching the telescope.

understand.summary: The Mayall telescope's Mosaic-3 camera observed the nebula in visible light through filters for oxygen III, hydrogen-alpha and the i band. The colour mapping isn't published.
filters: 502 nm · Optical OIII (NSF Nicholas U. Mayall 4-meter Telescope Mosaic-3)
657 nm · Optical H-alpha (NSF Nicholas U. Mayall 4-meter Telescope Mosaic-3)
772 nm · Optical i (NSF Nicholas U. Mayall 4-meter Telescope Mosaic-3)
understand.eye: The nebula is far too faint for the eye to see in this detail, and a long camera exposure gathers much more light than the eye can.

explore: It was the Mayall telescope's final image before DESI, the Dark Energy Spectroscopic Instrument, went in, and the Crab had also been its first target at first light in 1973. The Crab Pulsar was the first to connect a historical supernova with a pulsar of precisely known age.
